entry.title: Hess and Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission (Compensation) [2026] ARTA 2343
entry.content:
Martin Hess sought compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation (Defence-related Claims) Act 1988 (Cth) for lumbar spondylosis allegedly caused by his Australian Army Reserve service. The Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission denied liability, and Mr Hess sought review by the Tribunal. The Tribunal affirmed the denial because it was not satisfied that military service contributed to a significant degree to the condition.

Key holding: For a disease to be compensable under the DRCA, the employee’s employment must have contributed to the ailment to a significant degree, meaning substantially more than material.

significant degree" means a degree that is substantially more than material.

entry.title: Latif and Commissioner of the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2342
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission’s application to dismiss Mr Latif’s review applications concerning deemed internal review decisions to affirm a permanent ban and registration renewal refusal for Horizon Solsolutions Australia Pty Ltd. The case concerned whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction, whether Mr Latif was “directly affected”, and whether deemed decisions arose under the ART Act. The dismissal application was dismissed, so the substantive review applications remain on foot.

Key holding: A decision-maker cannot isolate a separate non-reviewable “standing” decision from the NDIS Act s 100 internal review process; standing is a threshold matter within that process and may be assessed by the Tribunal in determining jurisdiction.

It is my characterisation that the issue of standing is inherently a threshold matter that should be addressed as an integral part of the internal review process under s 100 of the NDIS Act, rather than as a distinct and, in this case as submitted by the Respondent, a non-reviewable decision made under s 100(2) of that Act.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.

Key holding: When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

entry.title: Application by CFMEU (105N) [2026] FWC 4041
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined on the papers a CFMEU application under s.437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 for a protected action ballot order for employees of M Maintenance Services Pty Ltd. The employer did not substantively object, and the Commission was satisfied the s.443(1) requirements were met. The main issue was the ballot closing date, which the Commission set for 30 October 2026 after applying CEPU v Nilsen.

Key holding: In setting the ballot period under s.443(3)(c), the Commission must establish a period that enables the ballot to be conducted as expeditiously as practicable.

Section 443(3A) of the Act requires the Commission to establish a ballot period that enables the ballot to be conducted as expeditiously as practicable.

entry.title: Mr Matthew Vickers v ASC Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4039
entry.content:
Mr Matthew Vickers made a general protections application under s.365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after ASC Pty Ltd dismissed him on 23 April 2025. He filed on 22 October 2025, 161 days after the 21-day statutory limit expired. The Fair Work Commission refused an extension of time under s.366(2), finding no exceptional circumstances.

Key holding: An applicant seeking an extension under s.366(2) must provide credible reasons for the delay; absent credible reasons, exceptional circumstances will not be established.

The absence of credible reasons for the delay advanced by Mr Vickers for filing his claim weigh heavily against a finding that exceptional circumstances exist in this case.

entry.content:

entry.title: Rebecca Ladner v Department of Home Affairs [2026] FWC 4029
entry.content:
Ms Rebecca Ladner applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against the Department of Home Affairs, 336 days outside the 21-day time limit. The Fair Work Commission considered whether to extend time under s 394(2)–(3). It found no exceptional circumstances and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A very lengthy delay weighs strongly against exceptional circumstances, particularly where the applicant had already filed an unfair dismissal application in time but discontinued it to pursue other options.

Having made findings on the factors in s 394(3) and considering them together, I am not satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. I have given particular weight to the length of the delay, and the fact that Ms Ladner had filed an unfair dismissal application within time, but chose to discontinue it in favour of other options.

entry.title: Ms Lisa Nothelfer v Hornibrook Bus Lines Pty. Ltd. [2026] FWC 3943
entry.content:
Lisa Nothelfer was found to have been unfairly dismissed by Hornibrook Bus Lines Pty Ltd in an earlier liability decision ([2026] FWC 2049). In this remedy decision, Deputy President Butler determined the matter on the papers, found reinstatement inappropriate and compensation appropriate, and awarded compensation under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Commission assessed compensation using s 392(2) and the Sprigg approach, fixing $24,050.20 gross.

Key holding: Under s 390(3) of the Fair Work Act, compensation in lieu of reinstatement may be ordered only if the Commission is satisfied that reinstatement is inappropriate and that compensation is appropriate in all the circumstances.

Under section 390(3) of the Fair Work Act, the Commission must not order the payment of compensation to the Applicant unless the Commission is satisfied that reinstatement of the Applicant is inappropriate, and the Commission considers an order for payment of compensation is appropriate in all the circumstances of the case.

entry.title: Mr Hossein Nasiri v Hendrickson Asia Pacific Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3929
entry.content:
Mr Nasiri applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) alleging unfair dismissal after Hendrickson Asia Pacific Pty Ltd terminated his employment on 29 May 2026 for alleged serious misconduct. The Commission found the Applicant lacked credibility, preferred the Respondent’s witnesses, and held there was a valid conduct-based reason with no s 387 factor favouring unfairness. Application dismissed: Nasiri v Hendrickson Asia Pacific Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3929.

Key holding: A dismissal is not harsh, unjust or unreasonable under s 387 where the Commission finds a valid conduct-based reason and none of the statutory matters weigh in favour of unfairness.

None of the factors set out in s 387 of the Act weigh in favour of the conclusion that the termination of The Applicant's employment was unfair.

entry.title: Vlasios Rotziokos v Futuresleep Pty/ Ltd [2026] FWC 4040
entry.content:
In Vlasios Rotziokos v Futuresleep Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4040, the Fair Work Commission considered an unfair dismissal application by a casual production worker dismissed after removing his safety vest and singlet on the factory floor during a meal break. The Commission found there was a valid reason for dismissal and a fair process, and that inconsistent enforcement of a related PPE colour requirement did not outweigh those matters. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: A dismissal for a clear safety-policy breach is not unfair where there is a valid reason, procedural fairness and prior specific warnings, even if the employer inconsistently enforced a related aspect of the policy, provided that inconsistency is outweighed by the other s 387 matters.

It follows from the above that having considered each of the matters specified in s.387 of the Act, I am satisfied that the dismissal of the Applicant was not harsh, unjust, or unreasonable. That is because there was a valid reason for the dismissal , the process followed by the Respondent was procedurally fair, the Applicant had been previously warned in relation to the specific conduct, all of which outweighs the inconsistent application of the Procedure I have identified.

entry.title: Application by Parminder Singh [2026] FWC 3947
entry.content:
Mr Parminder Singh applied under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair deactivation remedy after Uber permanently deactivated his driver account on 25 February 2026 following two touting complaints. The Commission found Uber failed to comply with the Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code and that there was no valid reason for the deactivation. It ordered reactivation and restoration of lost pay.

Key holding: For s 536LF(c), consistency with the Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code requires complete compliance with the Code, not merely substantial compliance.

We do not accept, for the purpose of the consideration required under s 536LF(c), that consistency with the Code tolerates less than complete compliance with it. Section 536LJ(3) makes it clear that consistency with the Code requires compliance with it.

entry.title: Application by Dsv Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4042
entry.content:
DSV Pty Ltd applied under s.120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 to reduce Ms Helen Priest’s redundancy pay to nil after losing its Laverton warehouse contract. DSV offered her an equivalent full-time role at its Truganina site, 6.8 km away, which she rejected before later changing her mind. The Fair Work Commission granted the application.

Key holding: Under s.120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment is acceptable is judged objectively, not by the employee’s subjective preference, and the Commission may exercise its discretion to reduce redundancy pay where such employment was obtained.

In relation to s.120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment obtained by the employer is "acceptable" is to be determined objectively, not by reference to whether the employment is subjectively acceptable to the employee. The determination of whether alternative employment is acceptable requires an assessment and value judgment on the part of the decision -maker.

entry.title: Dorothy Lazenkas v Mondelez Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWCFB 280
entry.content:
Ms Lazenkas made an unfair dismissal application, then later filed a general protections application in which she stated she withdrew the earlier unfair dismissal claim. The Full Bench considered whether s 725 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) barred the general protections application because the earlier application had not been withdrawn before the second application was made. By majority, the appeal was dismissed, with Vice President Gibian dissenting.

Key holding: Under the Fair Work Act, if an unfair dismissal application has been made, it must have been withdrawn before a subsequent s 365 general protections application is made; simultaneous withdrawal in the later application does not disengage s 725.

We do not consider that the language and structure of ss 725 and 729(1)(b)(i) can accommodate the simultaneous making of a second prescribed application and a withdrawal of a first. The withdrawal must precede the second application.

entry.title: Foong v Health Care Complaints Commission [2026] NSWCA 217
entry.content:
Dr Andrew Foong sought leave to appeal from NCAT’s refusal to recuse Principal Member Ainslie-Wallace AM ADCJ in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Health Care Complaints Commission. The alleged apprehended bias arose because the Principal Member had sat on a Medical Tribunal in 2010 with Dr Emery Kertesz, who was the Commission’s sole expert witness in the current proceedings. The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: A prior tribunal association with an expert witness will not, without more, create a reasonable apprehension of bias where the only feared influence is a favourable view of that expert’s expertise, and the expert’s credibility and relevant expertise are not in issue.

Here, the only relevant possibility was that the Principal Member had, by reason of prior association, formed and retained an attitude that Dr Kertesz had the expertise to give evidence as a general practitioner in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Commission against another general practitioner. This attitude had no potential to have any effect in the present proceedings as Dr Kertesz's expertise as a general practitioner was accepted.

entry.title: Manjunath and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2340
entry.content:
This Tribunal decision concerns an NDIS review application where the Applicant sought to add further supports shortly before a scheduled hearing. The Tribunal adjourned the hearing to allow the Respondent time to consider the late additions and, under s 53 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), fixed the issues in dispute. No final merits decision on the NDIS supports was made.

Key holding: The Tribunal may determine the scope of review by limiting the questions of fact, evidence and issues it considers.

In a proceeding for review of a decision, the Tribunal may determine the scope of the review by limiting the questions of fact, the evidence and the issues that it considers.

entry.title: Mishra and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2327
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of Mr Mishra’s Subclass 155 Five-Year Resident Return visa under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). In accordance with s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), the Tribunal must therefore consider whether there is another reason to exercise the discretion under s 501CA(4) to revoke the original decision.

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

The Guidance and Appeals Panel reviewed an ART decision that had found funding for an Orangutan Plus Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories to be a reasonable and necessary NDIS support for NGVL, a child with Autism and ADHD. The Panel focused on whether the equipment was “standard indoor or outdoor play equipment” excluded by item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules.

Key holding: Standard outdoor play equipment falling within item 4(p) of Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules is not an NDIS support and cannot be funded unless it is modified or adapted to address the participant’s functional impairments.

For the reasons given below, the Panel concludes that the Funky Monkey Bars Frame and accessories are 'standard...outdoor play equipment' and are therefore an excluded support under item 4(p) in Schedule 2 of the Transitional Rules. On this basis it cannot be included for funding in NGVL's SOPS.

entry.title: LFQR and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2320
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a refusal to pay family tax benefit top ups and supplements for 2022/23 because the applicant’s partner lodged his income tax return on 4 July 2024, after the 30 June 2024 reconciliation deadline. The applicant relied on stress, family violence, alcohol issues, a brief separation and pandemic-related pressures. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no special circumstances that prevented the partner from lodging on time.

Key holding: Under s 32D(1)(c)(ii) of the Administration Act, special circumstances will only extend the reconciliation time if they actually prevented the partner from lodging the income tax return by the required date.

For the Applicant to be paid top ups and supplements of family tax benefit for 2022/23, the Tribunal must be satisfied that there are special circumstances that prevented the Applicant's partner from lodging his income tax return by 30 June 2024.

entry.title: Mr Brogan Yorston v NRR Services Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3112
entry.content:
Mr Yorston had already been found to be unfairly dismissed after the Commission rejected NRR Services Pty Ltd’s genuine redundancy defence. This subsequent decision concerned compensation only. The Commission awarded 26 weeks’ pay plus superannuation, after finding he would likely have remained in a redeployed Operator role until the administrator’s appointment.

Key holding: Compensation for unfair dismissal is capped at 26 weeks’ pay under the Fair Work Act, even if the likely lost employment period is longer.

However, on the basis that the maximum compensation under the FW Act is 26 weeks.

entry.title: Police Federation of Australia (200V) v The Chief Commissioner of Police - Victoria Police [2026] FWC 3946
entry.content:
The FWC determined a s 739 dispute between TPAV and Victoria Police about whether two injured employees on AMUP were entitled to continued COT and DA allowances after their secondments to the DST ended. Commissioner Fox held that non-payment was consistent with cl 77 of the enterprise agreement because those allowances were not ordinarily payable in the employees’ substantive positions once the secondments ceased.

Key holding: Clause 77 AMUP does not require continued payment of position-specific allowances after the temporary secondment attracting them ends; “full pay” reflects what the employee would ordinarily have received absent AMUP.

Having considered the words, context and purpose, I do not accept that the relevant allowances continue to be payable upon the cessation of the secondment to DST.
